rows.description: The manager sees them separately, then together, asking each for facts, impact and what they need. Focusing on the work problem and the future, not on character, allows real listening.
graph_context: previous stage: Open clash
next stage: Clear agreements and follow-through
this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22

rows.description: They agree on who owns what, how credit is shared and how to raise concerns early. Both check in after a month, and the conflict serves as a lesson in speaking up sooner.
graph_context: previous stage: Mediated conversation
this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22

rows.description: A teenager sends "fine, whatever" after a friend cancels plans, meaning only mild disappointment. Without tone of voice or face, short words are easy to read as anger.
graph_context: next stage: The receiver fills the gap
this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: disappointment, anger

rows.subtype: Stage 2: The receiver fills the gap [Receiver]
rows.description: The friend reads coldness and thinks "she is furious at me." Uncertainty is uncomfortable, so the mind supplies the worst explanation and treats it as fact.
graph_context: previous stage: An ambiguous message
next stage: A defensive reply
this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: anger

rows.description: He sends a curt "ok, sorry I have a life too", which sounds like an attack. The first sender now feels truly hurt, and the misreading gets a real reason to exist.
graph_context: previous stage: The receiver fills the gap
next stage: Screenshots and outside opinions
this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: hurt

rows.description: Each shows the chat to friends who say "that is rude" and take sides. Advice from people who only hear one version firms up the conflict and adds new grievances.
graph_context: previous stage: A defensive reply
next stage: Moving to voice
this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: grief

rows.description: One says "Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other." Hearing a tone of voice usually dissolves half of the hurt within minutes, and laughter often follows.
graph_context: previous stage: Screenshots and outside opinions
next stage: A habit for next time
this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: amusement, hurt

rows.subtype: Stage 6: A habit for next time [Response]
rows.description: They agree to ask "what did you mean?" before reacting and to call when something feels off. They learn that a text is only words on a screen, and that a pause is better than a quick reply when hurt.
graph_context: previous stage: Moving to voice
this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: hurt

rows.subtype: Stage 1: A terse message in a busy hour [Actor]
rows.description: A husband, in a meeting, texts "will be late, don't wait" and forgets to add that a friend is unwell. His wife receives it, already tired from her own day, as one more sign of being unimportant.
graph_context: next stage: Interpretation through old hurts
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
related mind states: tiredness

rows.description: She recalls other late nights and reads the text as a pattern. Old grievances colour a neutral message, and the actual sentence matters less than the story she attaches to it.
graph_context: previous stage: A terse message in a busy hour
next stage: A cold reply, a colder one
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
related mind states: grief, hurt
